rationale: The book's core reading of valley as the low and humbled (the status opposite mountain-kingdoms) is the best-supported account of the only texts it actually cites and of the mountain symbol established across Daniel, Revelation, Isaiah and Jeremiah. Isaiah 40:4's parallel ('every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low') is explained cleanly once mountain = kingdom: the high powers are humbled and the lowly raised. The trial/suffering reading (the dominant common view) has no purchase on that parallel or on the multi-text mountain pattern, and therefore cannot be the superior explanation of the supplied evidence. Secondary elaborations ('enslaved by the mountains,' 'obedient even to death') are natural extensions of the same opposition and do not introduce unsupported steps.
book_core_identification: the low and humbled (people or status), opposite of the mountain-kingdom
book_secondary_elaborations: the humble who are obedient even to death and will therefore be exalted
strongest_counter_interpretation: Valley most commonly symbolizes a season of trial, suffering, darkness or spiritual low point (the 'low place' of human experience) through which God nevertheless accompanies the believer, driven chiefly by Psalm 23:4 and reinforced by the Valley of Baca and similar images.
counter_core_identification: a low place or season of trial, suffering, grief or spiritual darkness
material_core_denial: that the symbol's primary referent is the lowly/humbled people or status rather than a place or period of hardship
counter_case: Psalm 23:4 ('valley of the shadow of death') is the most frequently cited text and is almost universally read as mortal danger, grief or dark trial with divine presence
Psalm 84:6 (Valley of Baca) is read as a place of weeping or hardship transformed by pilgrimage
Ezekiel 37 valley of dry bones is read as extreme desolation from which God restores
popular Christian preaching, hymnody and devotion treat 'valley' as the dark season of life, not as a social class opposite kingdoms
book_explanatory_advantages: derives valley directly and consistently from the well-attested mountain = kingdom symbol via the explicit opposition in Isaiah 40:4
explains the precise parallel structure of Isaiah 40:4 (valleys exalted / mountains made low) as the humbling of kingdoms and the raising of the lowly
fits the book's multi-witness method without contradiction among the mountain texts supplied (Daniel 2, Revelation 17, Isaiah 2, Jeremiah 51, etc.)
gives a single coherent referent that unifies the leveling imagery with the rest of the mountain symbol system
counter_explanatory_advantages: accounts for the dominant devotional and homiletic use of the word across Christian tradition
fits several named valleys whose narrative settings involve death, weeping or desolation
Psalm 23 is cited far more often for the symbol than Isaiah 40:4
decisive_sources: Daniel 2:35, 44-45 (stone becoming a mountain that fills the earth = kingdom)
Isaiah 2:2 / Jeremiah 51:25 (mountain of the Lord's house; destroying mountain)
unresolved_objections: the book never re-reads the primary trial texts (Psalm 23:4, Valley of Baca, dry bones) under its definition, leaving open whether those passages can be integrated or must be treated as non-symbolic
many biblical valleys function as ordinary geographical place-names with no evident symbolic load

the humility/lowliness reading is already listed as a recognized alternative in common teaching, so the book's divergence is mainly from the primary trial convention rather than from every existing reading
